subject: Logistic models (hierarchical and regular) for rare event data

messages.author: 9380fccf66859560
messages.subject: Logistic models (hierarchical and regular) for rare event data
parts:
Dear Stan list,

I write you today just to ask if anyone would know of any Stan code implementing a model for binary logistic regression in the case of rare event data (i.e. when the 1s are very rare in comparison to the 0s in the outcome variable). I have been searching for any solution in that direction, be it in a regular or in a hierarchical framework. Any suggestions or references will be very much appreciated.

Thanks for your time,

Martina Andrews

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Logistic models (hierarchical and regular) for rare event data
parts:
Just the regular logistic regression code in the Stan manual should work fine.  You just want to add informative priors for the coefficients because of possible separation.  Something like beta ~ student_t(1,0,2.5) is a weak prior that should be a good starting point assuming your predictors have been scaled to be of order 1.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Logistic models (hierarchical and regular) for rare event data
parts:
> On Apr 4, 2015, at 5:36 PM, martina...@gmail.com wrote:

> Many thanks for the prompt reply. That's an elegant solution, in fact. I wonder however to which extent it will be able to deal with the risk of underestimation of the effect of the variables of interest upon the Pr(Y=1).

Underestimation is a form of bias where the expected value
of a parameter is less than the true value. I think what
you're worried about is Pr[Y_n = 1 | data] being too low for cases
where Y_n = 1, which isn't quite the same thing.

In machine learning terms, Bayesian posteriors are based on
log loss, which is much less sensitive to category imbalance than
something like naive Bayes. Even so, the overall objective function
is the log probabilty of the true categories given the model, so it
can still be an issue.

One thing you can do is artificially inflate the counts of one category
by repeating instances. The effect is to overweight the overcounted
instances in the fit. This will, in general have the opposite effect.

> I will play around with some prior specifications to see what happens. In any case, let me just ask a quick theoretical follow-up. If my predictors have not been scaled to be of order 1, then the best parameters for the informative prior in this case would be my expected value for the coefficient with a small sigma (but not too small so to approach the uninformative-ness)?

You want the prior to match what you expect the posterior to be.
If it's too small, it'll be overly informative, not uninformative,
but maybe you're thinking in terms of the BUGS/JAGS precision parameters.

- Bob

your model with simulated data to get a feeling for what
category imbalance will do to your estimates.
